extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers seeking guidance on manners, social conduct, and the idea of the 'gentleman'
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic guide to what constitutes a 'gentleman' and the principles of good society and manners — describing personal qualities, social practices, and the role of fashion and selection in polite life.

rubrics_metrics.name: The gentleman is a man of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “The gentleman is a man of truth, lord of his own actions, and expressing that lordship in his behavior, not in any manner dependent and servile, either on persons, or opinions, or possessions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manners must be grounded in honesty and self-mastery rather than deference or servility. Truth is the fundamental point of courtesy: a gentleman does not dodge, but meets another frankly (hands, eyes, direct greeting). Anti-patterns: skulking, dissimulation, excessive deference to persons or fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal force / original energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Power and original energy are first requisites of the leading class: a gentleman “points at original energy” and is “a man standing in his own right and working after untaught methods.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders in society show animal spirits, initiative, boldness, and the capacity to act effectively in politics, trade, or other arenas. Examples cited: Saladin, Julius Caesar, Alexander. Anti-patterns: timid formality, mere talkers and clerks without initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature / benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond truth and force, the gentleman’s character “denotes good-nature or benevolence: manhood first, and then gentleness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social success rests on heartiness and sympathy — the power to fill and 'content' the company. Examples: Fox’s generosity, rescuing a drowning man, philanthropic acts. Anti-patterns: uncomfortable egotism, absence of sympathy, which make even capable persons socially unsuccessful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners facilitate life — remove impediments
rubrics_metrics.description: “Manners aim to facilitate life, to get rid of impediments and bring the man pure to energize. They aid our dealing and conversation as a railway aids travelling, by getting rid of all avoidable obstructions of the road.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good manners are functional: they smooth interaction, prevent misunderstandings, and make fellowship possible. They are a social technology, not mere ornament. Anti-patterns: manners that intimidate or obstruct fellowship rather than assist it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composure and self-content
rubrics_metrics.description: “All that fashion demands is composure and self-content.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A gentleman maintains calmness, self-possession, and an ease that lets his native manners show. Even if one lacks other graces, composure and confidence often carry social acceptance. Anti-patterns: giddiness, awkwardness, visible insecurity in new situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference and stateliness (measured independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emerson prefers a tendency to stateliness and deference: “I like that every chair should be a throne, and hold a king... Let us not be too much acquainted. I would have a man enter his house through a hall filled with heroic and sacred sculptures... We should meet each morning as from foreign countries.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respectful distance, measured deference, and preserving a person’s individuality (the island of a man inviolate) are virtues. Lovers should guard their strangeness. Anti-patterns: excessive familiarity that erodes dignity and leads to meanness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospitality — the house needs a master
rubrics_metrics.description: Old feudal etiquette: a gentleman receiving a visit “should not leave his roof, but should wait his arrival at the door of his house... No house... is good for anything without a master.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True hospitality requires the host’s presence and mastery — the host should own and embody his household rather than hide behind screens (luxuries, ornaments). Anti-patterns: house as mere display with no masterly reception; using screens to avoid full encounter with guests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of beauty / taste / love of measure
rubrics_metrics.description: “We imperatively require a perception of, and a homage to beauty in our companions... The love of beauty is mainly the love of measure or proportion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine manners require taste and refined perception — accuracy and proportion temper brilliance. Society values those who practice measure rather than extremes. Anti-patterns: screaming, overuse of superlatives, conversational heat and sharp points that drive people away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in precision — leave business omniscience at the door
rubrics_metrics.description: One may be “too punctual and too precise. He must leave the omniscience of business at the door, when he comes into the palace of beauty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive exactness and businesslike scrutiny offend in social settings; social intelligence tolerates some slowness and reserve. Anti-patterns: behaving as in business meetings or showing excessive pedantry in convivial company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellect plus moral perception in good-breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: “To the leaders of men, the brain as well as the flesh and the heart must furnish a proportion. Defect in manners is usually the defect of fine perceptions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-breeding combines intelligence, morality, and perception; manners without insight are hollow. The polite person has both kindness and a refined sense of fit and proportion. Anti-patterns: coarse lack of perception, crude behavior despite outward polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity and public-spirited action
rubrics_metrics.description: True gentility is shown in deeds: “There is still ever some admirable person... who jumps in to rescue a drowning man;... some absurd inventor of charities; some guide and comforter of runaway slaves...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical generosity, civic action, charitable projects, and enduring public service distinguish the genuine gentleman from mere fashion. Anti-patterns: empty civility with no real generosity; fashion’s mimicry of benevolence without substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion as a symbolic institution — organizes beauty but excludes pretenders
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashion is both a product and organizer of cultivated manners: “Fashion... is a self-constituted aristocracy... a select society... perpetuates itself... It rests on reality, and hates nothing so much as pretenders.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fashion selects and refines social forms and can reward genuine merit, but it also contains frivolity and transient fads. It excludes pretenders, yet may admit ephemeral monsters of the day. Anti-patterns: confusing mere fashionable show for real merit; relying on novelty alone for status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding pretension; sincerity over affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashion delights to “exclude and mystify pretenders and send them into everlasting 'Coventry.'” A gentleman’s badge is a natural, not an acquired, dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincerity and intrinsic worth trump superficial polish. The social community detects and castigates pretence; authenticity tends to be admitted even from unexpected sources (e.g., Jock the teamster in a crisis). Anti-patterns: calculated affectation, social climbing by mimicry without substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners as social selection and reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Society perpetuates a select fraternity: it 'colonizes every new-planted island and adopts and makes its own whatever personal beauty or extraordinary native endowment anywhere appears.' Fashion and aristocracy are mutual selections and tenacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social groups form and maintain distinctions by repeated selection; natural claims and symmetrical social qualities open doors. Awareness of this helps one navigate social advancement: cultivate real sympathies and capacities rather than mere trappings. Anti-patterns: expecting legal or formal sanction to produce social standing where no natural claim exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between individuality and social blending
rubrics_metrics.description: Society 'hates corners and sharp points of character' but values peculiarities that are consistent with fellowship; the ideal is a fellow who 'exactly fill[s] the hour and the company; contented and contenting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be original but socially adaptable: personal genius or peculiarity is prized when it refreshes and harmonizes with company. Anti-patterns: abrasive individuality that obstructs blending and damages fellowship.
